case.case_title: Amunupura Seelawansa Thero and others v Additional Secretary, Public Service Commission and others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, SC FR 575/2003, decided on 23 November 2004

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioners' fundamental rights under Article 12(1) were violated by the respondents' decision to cancel their promotions while allowing similarly circumstanced officers to be promoted.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioners argued that their Article 12(1) rights were violated because they were denied promotions to Class I of the SLTES while other officers similarly circumstanced were promoted and their promotions were not cancelled, constituting arbitrary and discriminatory treatment.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the petitioners did not meet the mandatory requirement of five years satisfactory service in Class II Grade I at the time of application, unlike the officers promoted earlier, and that the petitioners and the other officers applied for promotions at different times and under different conditions, thus no discrimination occurred.
key_facts: Petitioners applied for promotion to Class I of SLTES in 2001 after only one year of service in Class II Grade I.
Petitioners were initially promoted with effect from 15.05.2002 but promotions were later cancelled.
Nine other officers were promoted to Class I in 1999 with backdated appointments and their promotions were not cancelled.
The mandatory requirement for promotion was five years satisfactory service in Class II Grade I and confirmation in that grade.
Petitioners did not fulfill the five-year service requirement at the time of application.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court held that Article 12(1) guarantees equal treatment in the performance of lawful acts, not the execution of illegal acts. Equal opportunity applies to equals similarly circumstanced, and unequals cannot be treated as equals. The requirement of five years satisfactory service was a valid classification and condition for promotion.
reasoning.application_to_facts: Since the petitioners did not meet the basic qualification of five years satisfactory service in Class II Grade I at the time of their application, their promotions were rightly cancelled. The court rejected the petitioners' reliance on earlier promotions of others who did not meet the criteria, emphasizing that authorities cannot be compelled to act illegally just because they acted illegally before.
principles_established: Equal protection under Article 12(1) applies only to lawful acts.
Valid classification based on service requirements is not discriminatory.
Authorities cannot perpetuate illegality to avoid discrimination.
Unequals cannot claim equal treatment as equals.
precedents_cited: C.W. Mackie and Co. Ltd. v Hugh Molagoda Commissioner-General of Inland Revenue and others 1986 1 Sri LR 300
Gamaethige v Siriwardane and others 1988 1 Sri LR 384
J.V. Setty v Commissioner, Corporation of the City of Bangalore AIR 1968 Mysore 251
Ram Prasad v Commissioner of India AIR 1979 Raj. 131
Chief Commissioner v Kitty Puri AIR 1973, Delhi 148

outcome.holding: The court dismissed the petitioners' claim that their Article 12(1) rights were violated, holding that the cancellation of their promotions was lawful and not discriminatory.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) was central to the petitioners' claim of discrimination in promotion. The court's reasoning focused on the proper interpretation of equal protection under this clause, emphasizing lawful treatment and valid classification, which directly determined the outcome.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioners did not fulfill the five years satisfactory service requirement at the time of application, and the court held that equal treatment guaranteed by Article 12(1) is equal treatment in the performance of a lawful act, not execution of an illegal act.
